video_title: Dylan Patel – Two labs will soon control most of the world's workforce
gist: Dylan Patel (SemiAnalysis) argues OpenAI and Anthropic are on track to consume roughly half the world's incremental compute by end of 2026 and ~100 combined gigawatts by 2028, with revenue per megawatt already having flipped from negative gross margin to $50M+ and heading toward $100M+; he makes the non-consensus call that labs will shift compute away from paying inference toward internal training/R&D, and frames regulation, credit-market crowding-out, and rising interest rates (not physics) as the real brakes on an otherwise runaway centralization of the world's effective labor supply into two companies.

insights.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic are taking roughly a third of all new global compute added in 2025 (both went from ~2GW to 5GW+, a 3-4x increase), and this share is projected to rise to 40-50% of incremental compute in 2026.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Compute allocation is becoming a two-buyer market; anyone selling AI infrastructure should model OpenAI/Anthropic as the marginal price-setters, not the broader hyperscaler market.

insights.claim: World compute in gigawatts is doubling roughly every year, but compute at the frontier labs is tripling every year, meaning the two labs' share of the global compute base is structurally destined to keep rising rather than plateau.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: A simple 2x-vs-3x growth-rate gap compounds fast; investors should expect lab compute share to keep climbing for years absent an external shock (regulation, capital constraints).

insights.claim: By the end of 2027, roughly half of the world's incremental new compute is projected to already be going to just OpenAI and Anthropic combined.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: A one-to-two-year timeline for hitting 50% share is aggressive; watch quarterly capex/compute disclosures from these two labs as the key leading indicator for the broader AI capex cycle.

insights.claim: If current trends hold, by end of 2028 the two labs could control over 100 combined gigawatts, and because that marginal compute runs on newer, 3-5x more efficient hardware (GB300, TPUv7, Trainium3), their effective share of the world's usable flops is even higher than their raw gigawatt share suggests.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Raw gigawatt counts understate real capability concentration; any competitive analysis of AI capacity needs a quality/efficiency adjustment, not just headline watts.

insights.claim: New entrants are increasingly building compute specifically to lease to the labs rather than to compete with them: SpaceX is emerging as a major compute builder that leases capacity to Anthropic and OpenAI, while OpenAI is building its own chips and Anthropic is deploying Google TPUs via Fluidstack.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: The supply side of AI compute is bifurcating into labs building/controlling their own stack versus balance-sheet-rich third parties (SpaceX, Meta) selling to labs at a premium — a distinct investable structure from generic 'hyperscaler capex' plays.

insights.claim: The base cost of AI compute is roughly $10-15 million per megawatt, and Anthropic's revenue per megawatt has already reached as high as $50 million — meaning $10 of compute spend can generate $50 of revenue that gets reinvested into training.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: This 4-5x markup is the entire engine funding the current AI capex boom; if it compresses (more competition, cheaper open models), the reinvestment flywheel breaks.

insights.claim: Anthropic began turning a profit in Q2, and OpenAI could turn profitable as soon as Q3, driven by Codex and GPT-5.6 growth — a shift from a year ago when both labs' spending was entirely venture-funded losses.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: The funding model for frontier AI is inflecting from pure VC subsidy to self-funded growth, which changes how much external capital these labs will need to raise going forward.

insights.claim: Dylan forecasts lab revenue per megawatt reaching $50M+ by end of 2027, potentially $70-80M blended across a company if best models keep shipping — a number Dwarkesh explicitly pushes back on as too conservative given the pace of model improvement.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: This is a testable, dated forecast; a rate of increase well above or below this trajectory is itself a signal about whether regulatory constraints or genuine RSI dynamics are dominating.
insights.quote: But I don’t see why it wouldn’t be $50-plus million a megawatt.

insights.claim: There is currently a 4x-or-greater gap between what a megawatt of compute sells for on the open market and how much revenue Anthropic can generate from that same megawatt internally — an inefficiency that has not yet been arbitraged away.
insights.speaker: Dwarkesh Patel
insights.so_what: As long as this gap persists, the labs (and whoever supplies them, e.g. SpaceX) will keep bidding compute prices up; the gap closing is itself a signal that the market is reaching equilibrium.

insights.claim: Roughly $6 billion of wafer-fab capital expenditure (equipment plus cleanroom and shell) produces one gigawatt of AI compute capacity per year, and that gigawatt can generate on the order of $100 billion of revenue annually — implying over $1 trillion of cumulative end AI revenue from that single $6B of fab capex over five years, a greater than 100x discrepancy even after accounting for data center, power, and middleman costs.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: This return spread is the fundamental reason capital keeps flooding into AI infrastructure regardless of near-term risk; it also explains why physical bottlenecks (not capital) are now the binding constraint.
insights.quote: That still means there’s a 100x discrepancy between fab CapEx and end revenue generated.

insights.claim: The actual physical bottleneck constraining AI compute buildout has narrowed down to something as specific as the mirrors used in ASML's EUV lithography machines; Carl Zeiss only recently raised its own production target to roughly 100 EUV tools' worth of mirrors per year by 2030, and even that may be too conservative given the economics.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: A single component supplier (Carl Zeiss mirror production) is a genuine chokepoint for the entire AI buildout — worth tracking as a leading indicator independent of chip or GPU headlines.

insights.claim: Demand for compute is so acute that arbitrage has already emerged around scarce physical inputs: people are buying power turbines and reselling them at a premium because a turbine's value as a data-center bottleneck-breaker now exceeds its equipment cost, and someone who could secure and resell an ASML EUV tool (roughly $400M) could plausibly flip it for north of $1 billion.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Secondary markets for capital equipment (turbines, EUV tools) are a real, current phenomenon — a tell that official capex/lead-time numbers are already stale relative to true scarcity pricing.

insights.claim: Supply-chain price adjustment to AI demand behaves like a bullwhip: TSMC raises prices very slowly while memory makers (SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung) and substrate companies reprice quickly, because compute buyers who successfully raise prices at one layer (e.g., Elon Musk/SpaceX selling compute at $25-40M+/megawatt instead of $13-15M) create a cascading incentive for suppliers further down the chain to also raise prices.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Expect differentiated pricing power and margin timing across the supply chain — memory and substrate names likely re-rate on AI pricing power faster than foundry names like TSMC.
insights.quote: So with the value capture, I think there’s a bullwhip effect here.

insights.claim: Headline 'AI capex' figures ($40-50B typically cited) only capture critical IT (servers, networking, transceivers) and exclude the data center shell and power generation infrastructure, which are 15-30-year assets that must be built years ahead of the compute they'll house — meaning true incremental capex could be $7-10 trillion per year by 2028-2030, roughly a quarter to a third of the current-size US economy.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Investors benchmarking 'AI capex' against reported IT spend are dramatically undercounting the true capital commitment already locked in via power plants and shells being built today for multi-year-out compute needs.

themes.theme: Value Capture Migration Across the AI Stack

insights.claim: Value capture in AI has migrated across layers over time: in 2023 memory makers captured almost none of the value from HBM despite its criticality; value then concentrated at the chip/fab layer while the model layer (labs) ran negative gross margins; today TSMC actually captures less value than the memory companies, and the model layer is swinging toward large positive margins.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Value-capture position in the AI stack is not fixed — it rotates by layer over 1-2 year windows, so long-only exposure to any single layer (fabs, memory, labs) carries real repricing risk both ways.

insights.claim: End customers currently capture more value from AI models than the labs themselves do: Jane Street (an exclusive/major customer of both OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Ultrafast mode and Anthropic) reportedly generates far more value per token than Anthropic earns in profit from selling it, and Meta — once rumored to be up to 10% of Anthropic's business — captures more value via ad-engagement optimization than Anthropic captures from serving it.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: The 'AI value capture' debate is currently being won by sophisticated end-users, not model providers — a reason to focus on best-in-class deployers of AI (trading firms, ad platforms) as much as on the labs themselves.

insights.claim: Elon Musk/SpaceX demonstrated a new power dynamic in the compute market by building compute on balance sheet without a locked-in customer, then selling short-term capacity to Anthropic and Google at $25-40M+ per megawatt (vs. the prevailing $13-15M contracted rate) — recouping full capex in about a year and revealing that hoarding uncommitted compute confers pricing leverage that traditional pre-financed data-center building does not.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Meta and SpaceX are positioned as the only plausible 'third parties' with the balance-sheet capacity to hoard compute and auction it opportunistically — a structurally different (and potentially more profitable) business model than being a contracted-in-advance cloud provider.

insights.claim: Despite the SpaceX spot-pricing precedent, most compute is expected to keep transacting below roughly $20 billion per gigawatt-equivalent even a year out, because the overwhelming majority of compute is still contracted and financed before it's built, limiting how much of the market can access auction-style pricing.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Spot/auction pricing headlines (like the SpaceX-to-Google deal) are the exception, not the emerging norm — most compute contracts should still be modeled off pre-negotiated rates, not the highest observed spot price.
insights.quote: I think most compute will still continue to transact at sub-$20 billion a gigawatt.

themes.theme: Non-Consensus Call: Training Will Eat Inference

insights.claim: Dylan's explicit non-consensus call is that labs will allocate a shrinking, not growing, share of compute to revenue-generating inference over time, because internal use of compute for AI research/training compounds into future capability and earnings power in a way that simply selling more inference tokens does not.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: This directly contradicts the standard sell-side assumption that inference will dominate long-run compute demand; if correct, it implies training-cluster capex (not inference-serving capacity) is the segment to size for continued hypergrowth.
insights.quote: The labs are going to allocate less and less compute to inference over time. I think that’s very non-consensus.

insights.claim: Evidence for the inference-to-training shift: Anthropic kept adding more compute month over month through the year, yet its ARR growth plateaued rather than continuing to skyrocket — implying the marginal megawatt is increasingly being routed to R&D rather than revenue-generating inference.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Watch the ratio of compute growth to ARR growth at the labs as a real-time indicator of this shift; a widening gap (compute up, ARR flat) is direct confirmation of the training-reallocation thesis.

insights.claim: The current lab compute budget breaks down as roughly 60% training / 40% inference, with the training share itself split into ~50% 'research' (experimentation on architectures, data mixes, hyperparameters) and ~10% actual model 'development'; a full pre-training run for a frontier model like Anthropic's next model ('Mythos') reportedly used under 200 megawatts for about two months, with the RL phase using even less at any single point in time despite higher cumulative compute.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Most of a lab's multi-gigawatt fleet is not actually bottlenecking on a single training run today (sub-200MW peak) — implying enormous headroom for either more parallel research experiments or, if multi-site training is solved, much larger single training runs.
insights.quote: It’s sub-200 megawatts for, call it, two months.

insights.claim: As labs go public and become accountable to investors, they will face direct pushback for diverting revenue-generating inference compute to training (e.g., forgoing tens or hundreds of billions in near-term revenue) — but Dylan expects both executives and boards to keep favoring training/AGI-building over near-term profit distribution because it is 'way more profitable' long-run.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: A public OpenAI or Anthropic that keeps sacrificing near-term revenue for training compute would be a highly unusual public-company capital-allocation stance — worth watching closely at any future IPO or investor day for this exact tension to surface.

insights.claim: In 2022, the US added roughly 45-50% of world AI compute and China roughly 30-35%; since then, export controls plus a US buildout surge have flipped this dramatically — today roughly 70% of global AI-datacenter watts are deployed in America while China is under 10% of incremental new compute.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: This is a large, measurable policy-driven shift in global compute share within roughly three years — a concrete data point for anyone modeling the US-China AI race or export-control efficacy.

insights.claim: China's current AI compute still relies heavily on smuggled or diverted chips — including TSMC-made chips sold to buyers later found to be Huawei-linked — and Samsung-sourced HBM, with meaningful domestic fab output (SMIC, CXMT) only expected to scale to millions of units per year starting in 2027-2028.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Domestic Chinese chip supply is a 2027-2028 story, not a today story — near-term China compute estimates should be built primarily around gray-market/diverted foreign chips.

insights.claim: China is projected to have at most ~30 gigawatts of AI compute by 2028, and even that overstates its real capability because domestically produced chips will be meaningfully worse than what Nvidia, Google, or OpenAI will have that year; China could add ~50 incremental gigawatts in 2029, but weighted for chip quality that is roughly equivalent to only ~20 gigawatts of American-chip compute.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: A quality-adjusted compute gap (not just raw gigawatts) is the right lens for comparing US and Chinese AI capability trajectories, and it implies the gap is wider than raw capacity figures suggest.

insights.claim: If this trajectory holds, a single leading US lab could have more usable compute by 2028 than all of China will have by 2029 or even 2030 once gigawatts are quality-weighted — implying that by the time the US reaches 'automated researcher' capability, China will be structurally far behind on compute stock, which Dylan (a self-described libertarian who previously steelmanned the anti-export-control case with Nvidia's Jensen Huang) now calls a 'notable success' for export controls.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: This is a genuine view update from someone previously skeptical of export controls, based on the compute math laid out in this conversation — a signal worth weighing for anyone modeling US semiconductor export policy efficacy.
insights.quote: Actually, the export controls do seem to have really… If they ship the amount that you’re saying, that’s a huge difference.

insights.claim: Part of China's compute gap versus the US reflects not just export controls but differing financial-system risk appetite: American finance is more willing to 'YOLO' capital into speculative startups, whereas Chinese state-directed finance, once it commits to an industry, subsidizes it far more heavily than the rest of the world's semiconductor industries combined — meaning a slower Western AI takeoff would let China close the gap faster via subsidy-driven scaling.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: The US compute lead is partly a function of AI-takeoff speed itself: a slower takeoff scenario is structurally more favorable to Chinese catch-up than a fast one, which should inform how investors weight geopolitical AI-race risk against takeoff-speed assumptions.

insights.claim: Despite the huge compute gap, leading Chinese labs (100-200 megawatts total compute, with ByteDance Seed as an outlier) are not perceived by the public to be far behind top US labs in model quality relative to the compute they have, and Dylan argues this compute gap 'doesn't matter that much' yet because so much of a lab's compute budget currently goes to research experimentation rather than the actual training run.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Chinese labs are currently punching above their compute weight, which suggests algorithmic/research efficiency — not raw compute — has been the binding constraint on frontier model quality so far, a dynamic that could change once training runs themselves start consuming a larger compute share.

themes.theme: Macro Risk: Debt, Interest Rates, and Sovereign Defaults

insights.claim: Modeling puts total hyperscaler/cloud AI capex at roughly $11 trillion from 2024-2029, with about $6 trillion coming from operating cash flow and roughly $5 trillion needing to be raised via debt — a real, quantified driver of upward pressure on credit market interest rates.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: A $5 trillion incremental credit issuance over five years is large enough to move rates on its own — credit investors should model hyperscaler/AI debt issuance as a macro variable, not just a sector-specific one.

insights.claim: Dylan 'vibes out' a forecast that hyperscaler borrowing costs could rise from the 5-6% Meta recently paid to roughly 8% by 2029, as AI capex financing needs crowd out other borrowers, implying a roughly 250 basis point widening that would pass through to the rest of the economy's credit costs as well.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Even a self-acknowledged 'vibed' number gives a scenario to stress-test: a 250bp systemic rate increase would meaningfully repricing credit-sensitive sectors (banks, telecom, consumer packaged goods) well before any AI-specific shock hits.
insights.quote: Dude, this is vibing a number, but if you’re vibing a number out…

insights.claim: Rising discount rates from AI-driven credit crowding-out would crater the valuations of long-duration, steady-cash-flow 'boring' stocks (Berkshire-Hathaway-type holdings, railways, Johnson & Johnson-style consumer staples) even while AI-exposed names and the broad S&P 500 index could remain fine in aggregate — implying a valuation rotation/dispersion event rather than a broad market crash.
insights.speaker: Dwarkesh Patel
insights.so_what: This argues for expecting significant dispersion under a rate-driven AI-capex scenario: short/underweight long-duration low-growth cash-flow compounders, rather than betting on a uniform market direction.

insights.claim: Citing economist Basil Halperin's framing of a 'second Volcker shock,' rising AI-driven real interest rates could trigger sovereign defaults among highly indebted, low-tax-revenue countries with frequent debt servicing needs — explicitly naming Pakistan and Nigeria as vulnerable — echoing the ~40 mostly-Latin-American country defaults triggered by Volcker's early-1980s rate hikes.
insights.speaker: Dwarkesh Patel
insights.so_what: AI capex-driven rate increases are being framed as a potential emerging-markets sovereign-debt catalyst, not just a US tech-sector story — a reason for EM-debt investors to watch AI capex financing volumes as a macro risk factor.
insights.quote: Those countries, like Pakistan or Nigeria, I think are just going to be very fucked in this new interest-rate regime.

insights.claim: The bull case for the US avoiding an AI-driven sovereign debt crisis rests on being able to tax AI/data-center activity domestically: currently under 10% of federal revenue is corporate income tax (80%+ is payroll/income tax, which shrinks as automation displaces workers), and roughly 20% of spending already services debt interest — a 1-point rate rise pushes that toward 25%, a 5-point rise toward 40%+, and combined with ~$2 trillion/year in new government borrowing could push debt service above 60% of tax revenue.
insights.speaker: Dwarkesh Patel
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, numbered scenario for US debt-service-to-revenue ratios under rising rates — useful as a stress-test framework for anyone modeling US fiscal sustainability against an AI-driven rate-hike scenario.

insights.claim: The real brake on the AI buildout is not physical capacity but credit-market crowding-out: AI capex competes for the same debt markets as governments, consumer-packaged-goods firms, telecoms, and banks, and this competition for capital — combined with regulation and political backlash — is what 'bends the curve' below what pure unconstrained capitalist economics would otherwise produce.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Frame AI capex growth limits primarily as a credit-market and political-economy constraint, not an engineering one — meaning bond market stress or a political backlash event is a more likely near-term brake than a physical supply-chain shortfall.
insights.quote: This crowding-out effect is the reason it’s not YOLO 1 billion gigawatts.

themes.theme: AI Labor Concentration and the Centralization Endgame

insights.claim: Even without recursive self-improvement (RSI), the effective 'AI population' (labor-equivalent capacity) at frontier labs is growing roughly 10x per year, driven by frontier compute (FLOPs) growing 4-5x annually while the compute needed to hit a given capability level falls roughly 3x annually.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: A 10x/year growth rate in effective AI labor supply, independent of any RSI breakthrough, is itself a major economic variable — this alone implies labor-market and wage effects should be modeled well before any singularity-style scenario.
insights.quote: the effective AI population size at the frontier labs is increasing 10x year over year

insights.claim: At current trends, a lab like OpenAI could go from roughly 10 million 'AI laborer' equivalents this year to 100 million next year to 1 billion the year after — and before the end of this decade, a single lab could plausibly command more labor-equivalent capacity than there are humans on Earth.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: If directionally correct, this reframes 'AGI risk' as an already-in-motion labor-supply-concentration story rather than a future hypothetical — worth tracking via any disclosed compute/capability scaling metrics from the labs.
insights.quote: there’s more AI labor, more effective population, within a single lab than there are people on Earth

insights.claim: Because most of the world's future work output risks concentrating inside just two labs, the alignment risk framing shifts: if these AI systems end up misaligned, 'most of the world is misaligned' by extension, since most cognitive/labor output will be running inside them — a framing distinct from typical single-company-takeover narratives.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: This reframes AI safety/alignment as a market-structure and antitrust-adjacent issue (labor-supply concentration), not purely a technical one — relevant to how regulators and investors should think about systemic risk from just two firms.

insights.claim: A recent public dispute referenced: Gavin Baker claimed Dario Amodei believes there will ultimately be only one AI company, which Anthropic's Sholto Douglas and Dario publicly denied saying — but Dylan argues the underlying RSI/economies-of-scale logic points toward centralization regardless of what was explicitly claimed.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Public statements from lab leadership downplaying centralization should be weighed against the structural economics Dylan lays out — the denial doesn't resolve the underlying dynamic.

insights.claim: Two reinforcing mechanisms drive AI-market centralization regardless of RSI: (1) training has strong economies of scale because the cost amortizes across billions of user sessions, and (2) whoever is even slightly ahead in capability can charge a higher markup for scarce compute and therefore out-bid rivals for the next increment of compute — a self-reinforcing flywheel toward the leader.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: These two mechanisms suggest market share in frontier AI compounds rather than mean-reverts — relevant for anyone assessing whether a challenger lab can realistically close a capability gap once one opens.

insights.claim: Today, most of the value created by frontier AI models is not captured by OpenAI or Anthropic but flows to end customers (Jane Street's trading edge, Meta's ad-engagement gains) — a dynamic Dylan calls the 'one saving grace' against total concentration, but one that fades as labs increasingly redirect compute internally toward R&D instead of selling it externally as inference.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: The current diffusion of AI value to end-users is a temporary feature of today's inference-heavy compute allocation, not a permanent structural check on lab power — expect this 'saving grace' to erode as the training-reallocation thesis plays out.
insights.quote: Why would I let Jane Street make all this money off of these degenerate options traders?

themes.theme: Regulation as the Real Brake on the Bull Case

insights.claim: Regulatory and safety-driven caution is already visibly capping lab output: OpenAI reportedly has not released a model called 'Astra,' paused training for two weeks, and Anthropic has not released what its own safety assessment refers to as 'Model 2' (widely believed to be the successor to its 'Mythos' model) — concrete evidence that labs are deliberately not shipping their most capable systems.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: This is the single biggest wildcard against the bullish revenue-per-megawatt trajectory: if regulatory caution persists or intensifies, monetization growth (and thus the whole capex flywheel) slows even if underlying model capability keeps improving internally.

insights.claim: Regulation of AI compute is increasingly local and supply-side: New York is banning data centers, Texas is holding moratoriums, and Ohio is attempting to require data centers to pay property tax for surrounding property within a radius — all of which reduce compute supply and raise costs, effects that get passed through to lab customers.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: State/local jurisdictional risk (siting bans, moratoriums, tax changes) is now a material and specific variable for data-center site-selection and capex planning — not just a generic 'political risk' hand-wave.

insights.claim: Regulation is asymmetric by geography: restrictions on releasing or deploying frontier US models slow down US labs far more than they slow Chinese open-source models, since China faces no comparable domestic pressure to restrict deployment.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: US AI safety regulation has a geopolitical opportunity cost that is rarely priced into the domestic policy debate — every deployment restriction on US labs is a relative gift to Chinese open-source competitors.

insights.claim: Dylan's central fear is not that AI slows down, but that regulation aimed at delaying public release (e.g., a mandated six-month wait before releasing a new model) could inadvertently let recursive self-improvement run unchecked internally during that window, leaving the external/public-facing AI ecosystem years behind the labs' actual internal capability rather than genuinely slowing capability growth.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: This reframes 'pause the release, not the research' as potentially the worst-case regulatory outcome — a case for prioritizing internal-use transparency/oversight over release-timing restrictions if one wants to avoid concentrated, unchecked capability gaps.
insights.quote: In that six months, they do recursive self-improvement internally. They just have all kinds of crazy shit happening in the company.

insights.claim: Anthropic reportedly had to stop giving its 'Mythos' model (or a closely related checkpoint) to foreign employees at one point, suggesting internal-use restrictions on frontier models — not just public release restrictions — are already happening in practice.
insights.speaker: Dylan Patel
insights.so_what: Internal-access restrictions (not just external release delays) are an emerging and under-discussed category of AI governance already in effect — worth tracking as a leading indicator of how far regulatory/security constraints will extend.
